Introduction

Starting a Hospice in Pennsylvania represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals with terminal illnesses while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Pennsylvania Department of Health (PA DOH), Division of Home Health, with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

With a complex market signal showing a recent 4.7% decline in providers but high, unmet demand in rural counties and among the 85+ population, Pennsylvania offers a market with significant opportunity for providers who can address service gaps. Reimbursement rates, such as the Medicare routine home care rate of approximately $173.88 per patient day, create a viable financial model for agencies prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice in Pennsylvania, from understanding the state’s regulations and licensing procedures to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Pennsylvania’s Hospice Regulations

  • Business Structure and Licensing

  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Pennsylvania’s Hospice Regulations

Pennsylvania regulates Hospice programs through the Pennsylvania Department of Health (PA DOH), Division of Home Health. This agency is responsible for overseeing licensure, conducting inspections, and ensuring compliance with state health and safety standards under the Health Care Facilities Act. Because the vast majority of hospice patients are Medicare beneficiaries, providers serving this population must also comply with federal frameworks, primarily the CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) and HIPAA.

The regulatory framework in Pennsylvania, guided by the federal CoPs, emphasizes patient-centered care, comprehensive pain and symptom management, interdisciplinary team (IDT) coordination, patient and family rights, and bereavement support. Mastering these core principles is essential for passing your initial licensure and certification surveys. Licenses in Pennsylvania typically require renewal every one year, contingent on a successful survey and continued compliance.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While hospice is a single license type in Pennsylvania, it is delivered through four distinct levels of care defined by CMS. Understanding these is crucial for operational planning and billing. Pennsylvania supports multiple hospice service delivery models, each with different staffing, documentation, and reimbursement requirements:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, provided in the patient’s place of residence (private home, assisted living, nursing facility). This involves intermittent visits from the interdisciplinary team.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of crisis to manage acute symptoms. This requires a minimum of 8 hours of direct nursing care in a 24-hour period, with at least 50% provided by an RN.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For pain or symptoms that cannot be managed in another setting. This care is provided in a Medicare-certified hospital, skilled nursing facility, or dedicated inpatient hospice unit.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care provided to give the patient’s primary caregiver a break. This is limited to five consecutive days at a time.

Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC). A new agency might start with a target ADC of 15-25 patients, while established agencies can serve over 100. Demand is strongest in rural and underserved communities where provider access has recently declined. The market also shows high demand for agencies that can serve patients with chronic progressive illnesses and establish strong hospital integration for seamless patient transitions. While urban centers like Philadelphia and Pittsburgh have more competition, lower-penetration regions in central and northern Pennsylvania may offer significant entry opportunities.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can serve patients, you must establish a proper legal and administrative foundation. Providers in Pennsylvania typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or an S-Corporation to protect personal assets. The key steps to formalize your business include:

  • Register your business entity with the Pennsylvania Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Pennsylvania Department of Health (PA DOH), Division of Home Health.

This application requires detailed information about your agency’s ownership, governing body, key personnel, and service area. You will also need to submit a full set of policies and procedures for review. The licensing timeline, from application submission to the initial survey and final approval, generally ranges from 6 to 12 months, depending on your agency’s readiness and the completeness of your submission. Following state licensure, you must undergo a Medicare certification survey to become eligible for reimbursement.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a sustainable hospice agency. Startup costs in Pennsylvania for a new hospice agency typically range from $150,000 to $350,000. This capital covers initial licensing fees, legal and consulting costs, office setup, electronic medical record (EMR) software, and, most importantly, the payroll needed to hire your core team before reimbursement begins.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your interdisciplinary team. Staffing represents 60-70% of total operational costs. Your revenue will come from the per diem rates paid by Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges include:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): ~$173.88 per patient day
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Billed hourly, with a full 24-hour day reimbursed at over $1,000.
  • General Inpatient (GIP) & Respite Care: Reimbursed at higher facility-based rates.

Profitability is directly tied to managing your patient census and operational costs. Providers operating at a target utilization of 85-90% of their staffed capacity can generally achieve 15-25% gross margins. Most new agencies should plan for a break-even point between 12 and 24 months after certification.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Unlike an assisted living facility, a hospice agency’s physical location is an administrative office, not a patient residence (unless you plan to build a dedicated inpatient unit, which is a separate, more complex undertaking). Your office must be a professional space that supports your team and protects patient information. Facility requirements include:

  • HIPAA-compliant environment with private spaces for patient-related discussions.
  • Secure, locked storage for physical patient records and medical supplies.
  • Sufficient office space for the Administrator, Director of Nursing, and other administrative staff.
  • A conference room large enough to hold mandatory weekly interdisciplinary team (IDT) meetings.
  • Compliance with local zoning ordinances and building codes.

Your location selection should consider accessibility for your staff, proximity to major referral sources like hospitals and large medical practices, and the availability of a clinical workforce in the surrounding area.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your interdisciplinary team is the heart of your hospice. CMS regulations mandate specific roles to ensure holistic patient care. Required roles typically include:

  • Medical Director: A physician (MD or DO) who provides medical oversight and certifies patient eligibility.
  • Administrator / Director of Nursing: An RN responsible for the day-to-day operations and clinical management of the agency.
  • RN Case Managers: Registered nurses who coordinate and manage the patient’s plan of care.
  • Social Workers: A Master of Social Work (MSW) is required to provide psychosocial support.
  • Spiritual Counselors / Chaplains: To address the spiritual needs of patients and families.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: To manage the mandatory bereavement program for families for up to 13 months after a patient’s death.
  • Hospice Aides: Certified nursing assistants who provide personal care under the supervision of an RN.
  • Volunteers: A hospice must use volunteers, whose time must equal at least 5% of total patient care hours.

Training is a major focus of regulatory surveys. All staff require initial orientation on the hospice philosophy, agency policies, infection control, and patient rights. Additionally, ongoing training is mandated, with at least 12 hours of continuing education annually for clinical staff to ensure they are current on best practices in pain and symptom management.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your agency cannot be licensed without a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures. These documents are the operational playbook for your agency and prove to regulators that you have a plan for providing safe, compliant care. Pennsylvania requires written policies covering:

  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Care Planning and Coordination
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Volunteer Program Management and Training
  • Bereavement Program Services
  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program
  • Infection Control and Exposure Plan
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan

Individual care plans are the cornerstone of hospice documentation. They must be developed by the IDG within 5 days of admission, reviewed at least every 15 days, and meticulously documented to reflect the patient’s changing needs and the services provided. These documents are the primary focus of any clinical record review during a survey.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising; it is about building trust and professional relationships within the local healthcare ecosystem. Referrals for hospice care typically come from:

  • Hospitals: Discharge planners, case managers, and palliative care teams are the number one source of referrals.
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs): For long-term residents who are declining.
  • Assisted Living Facilities: As residents’ care needs exceed the facility’s capabilities.
  • Physician Offices: Especially oncologists, pulmonologists, cardiologists, and neurologists who manage patients with life-limiting illnesses.
  • Home Health Agencies: When a patient’s condition becomes terminal rather than curative.

Successful providers focus on demonstrating their value through compliance, clinical excellence, responsiveness, and clear outcome documentation. Building a reputation as a reliable partner who can accept complex cases and communicate effectively with referring physicians is the most effective marketing strategy. The market data’s emphasis on hospital integration underscores the importance of developing strong relationships with local hospital systems.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight in Pennsylvania is continuous. Your agency will be subject to unannounced inspections from surveyors representing the PA DOH, Division of Home Health, and CMS contractors (such as an Accreditation Commission for Health Care (ACHC) or Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP) if you choose that path for certification). Inspections focus on clinical record reviews, staff and patient interviews, and observation of care.

Common deficiencies cited during hospice surveys often relate to documentation and process failures. These include:

  • Incomplete or inconsistent patient care plans.
  • Lack of documentation for required IDG meetings.
  • Medication management and reconciliation errors.
  • Failure to provide or offer all four levels of hospice care.
  • Inadequate supervision of hospice aides.

To avoid these pitfalls, you must implement a robust Continuous Quality Improvement (QAPI) program. Regularly auditing your own charts, tracking key performance indicators, and maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times are essential for long-term compliance and success.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Hospice in Pennsylvania?

The entire process, from business formation to receiving your license and Medicare certification, typically takes 6 to 12 months. After certification, it can take another 12 to 24 months to reach a sustainable patient census and achieve profitability.

  • What licenses are required?

You need a Hospice license from the Pennsylvania Department of Health (PA DOH), Division of Home Health. To receive payment for services, you must also achieve Medicare certification by passing a survey that verifies your compliance with the federal Conditions of Participation.

  • What reimbursement is available?

The primary source of reimbursement is the Medicare Hospice Benefit, which pays a per diem (daily) rate. The rate varies based on the level of care provided, with the most common being the Routine Home Care rate of approximately $173.88 per day. Pennsylvania Medicaid and most private insurance plans have a similar benefit structure.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice in Pennsylvania is a challenging but deeply rewarding venture. The market presents a clear need, especially in rural and underserved areas where access to end-of-life care is limited. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in building a strong clinical team, fostering referral relationships, and committing to a culture of compliance are positioned for long-term success and community impact.
